newsitem.title: IRAN: Khatami sees Iran policy link to foreign inflows.
newsitem.headline: Khatami sees Iran policy link to foreign inflows.

text.p: Iran's incoming president recognises a connection between its often hostile relations with other countries and the lack of foreign investment at home, an Iranian economist said on Friday.

President-elect Mohammad Khatami, a moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric who takes over in August, will inherit an economy that is improving despite three years of inflation consistently over 50 percent, high unemployment and other difficulties.

But foreign investment is still urgently needed in the oil industry, Iran's main hard currency earner. Technologies are outdated and if not upgraded will result in rapid depletion of the country's oil reserves, economists said.
"Economic reform and restructuring can only be realised in connection with domestic and foreign policy," Bijan Khajehpour, a Tehran management consultant and editor of Iran Focus monthly, said.
"Economists have been saying this for some time. Now it's coming from Islamic sources. Khatami recognises it."

The United States, which seeks to isolate Iran as a rogue nation, in 1995 banned U.S. business from trade and investment in Iran and last year armed President Bill Clinton with powers to impose sanctions on foreign firms which invest $40 million or more a year in Iran's oil and gas sectors.
U.S. magazine Business Week recently called the policy shortsighted, misguided and wrong, and said it was also hurting Washington's own long-term political and economic interests.
Iran is the world's third largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia and Norway and possesses the world's second largest reserves of gas after those of Russia.
"Sanctions against Iran can only be controlled and eventually eliminated through reforms of Iran's foreign policy and international relations," Khajehpour said.
"The failure to see the connection between Iran's foreign policy and relations with other countries and the lack of foreign investment in Iran has been a major problem."

The need for heavy investment in the oil industry over the next decade would demand foreign policy reforms, including normalisation of relations with the United States, ruptured since 1980 at the height of the U.S. embassy hostage crisis.
Although Khatami sees the need for foreign investment to revitalise the economy he is bound by the five-year economic plan begun in 1995 under President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.

The plan commits Iran to the gradual removal of state controls. But parliament, controlled by conservative clerics, forced Rafsanjani to reduce the requirement for foreign financing, restricted the privatisation of state-owned enterprises and guaranteed continued subsidies on basic items.
Khajehpour said U.S. sanctions had had a negative psychological effect on Iranians as well as foreigners.
"First, Iranians feel they're under pressure and things they want are not fully available to them, and foreigners are fearful of a clash with the Americans.
"Second, Iran's oil and gas industry has suffered badly and needs huge sums of investment and new technology."

He said officials had admitted that Iran had mismanaged its oil reserves by using water injection technology to extract crude -- cheaper and easier than the more expensive but more efficient gas injection method.
"Rafsanjani said last year if we don't modernise the oil will last only until 2010, but if we do, we'll have enough for 100 years," Khajehpour said.
Unexpectedly high revenues from an OPEC quota of 3.6 million barrels a day have raised Iran's annual oil earnings to $18 billion a year.

Coupled with a series of bilateral reschedulings, this has enabled the Islamic republic to meet all its foreign debt payments and achieve a positive balance of payments, earning rare praise from the International Monetary Fund.
Economists blame the failure of privatisation plans on the absence of political reforms alongside economic reforms.
"There is no space for the private sector to share power. From that angle I believe Khatami can make a difference. He is prepared to talk to the private sector," Khajehpour said.
"The new president is not going to deviate very much from Rafsanjani's policies and will stay in the centre," economist Fariborz Raisdana told Reuters.
"He has no will, ability or legitimacy to change the five- year plan. It will be a continuation of the policies established last year with structural adjustment as the main stream."
Raisdana said both Rafsanjani and Khatami wanted to invite foreign investment but neither the president nor Central Bank Governor Mohsen Nourbakhsh had been able to provide guarantees.

"Without foreign investment it is very difficult to overcome our economic problems. We have very good conditions for foreign investment: plentiful labour, cheap fuel, low taxes, free zones, and a million-and-a-half students in universities," he added.
